plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a 3D diagram illustrating the Riemann sum approximation used to define the double integral as a volume. A curved surface z = f(x, y) is shown in xyz-space above a region in the xy-plane; the base is gridded to represent a partition into subrectangles. A single representative rectangular parallelepiped is highlighted in orange: its base is a subrectangle with area Delta_Ak and sampling point (x*_k, y*_k) labeled, and its height is f(x*_k, y*_k), giving volume f(x*_k, y*_k) Delta_Ak. Annotations label Height f(x*_k, y*_k), Volume f(x*_k, y*_k) Delta_Ak, and Area Delta_Ak. The figure introduces the double integral as the limit of a Riemann sum of such parallelepiped volumes over all subrectangles as the partition is refined.

elements: z-axis vertical with arrowhead and label 'z' at top
y-axis horizontal to the right with arrowhead and label 'y'
x-axis receding toward lower-left (toward viewer) with arrowhead and label 'x'
translucent teal curved surface z = f(x, y) floating above the xy-plane with a wavy upper rim
label 'z = f(x, y)' at upper right
closed peanut/kidney-shaped base region outlined in teal-green lying in the xy-plane
grid of partition lines (subrectangles) drawn across the base region
one highlighted subrectangle (the base of the representative column) near the front-center of the region
translucent orange rectangular parallelepiped (column) rising vertically from that subrectangle up to the surface
red dashed vertical centerline running through the column from base to top
red dot at the top of the column on the surface and red dot at the base (the sample point)
annotation 'Height f(x*_k, y*_k)' at right with arrow pointing to the red dashed centerline
annotation 'Volume f(x*_k, y*_k) ΔA_k' at right with arrow pointing to the orange column body
annotation 'Area ΔA_k' at lower left with arrow pointing to the highlighted base subrectangle
annotation '(x*_k, y*_k)' at lower center with arrow pointing to the red base dot

Dragging the sample point (x*_k, y*_k) across the gridded base relocates the orange column and updates its height to f at that location, showing that each subrectangle contributes its own sampled height f(x*_k, y*_k)·ΔA_k to the total volume

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale 1 unit = 1. Base region is a peanut/kidney shape roughly spanning x ∈ [-1.4, 1.4], y ∈ [-1.2, 1.2] in the xy-plane (z=0), drawn as a closed teal-green outline #1aa88a with an interior grid of grey partition lines (Δx = Δy ≈ 0.4). The highlighted subrectangle sits near front-center at about (x*_k, y*_k) = (0.3, 0.2) with ΔA_k = 0.16. Default surface f(x,y) = 2 - x^2 - y^2 (peak 2 at origin, zero at radius √2 ≈ 1.41); render as a translucent teal mesh #7fd4d4 at ~0.45 opacity over x,y ∈ [-1.5,1.5]. The orange column #f0a840 (~0.45 opacity) rises from the subrectangle (footprint 0.4 × 0.4) up to z = f(x*_k, y*_k) ≈ 1.87 by default. Red dashed centerline #e03020 with red sphere dots (radius ~0.05) at top (on surface) and base. Axes black with arrowheads; z up to ~2.5, x and y to ~±2. Displayed readouts: Height = f(x*_k,y*_k), Volume = f(x*_k,y*_k)·ΔA_k, Area = ΔA_k, updated live. Annotation arrows are thin black curved lines from each text label to its target.
interactionPlan.notes: Use a standard isometric/axonometric pose matching the source (x toward lower-left, y right, z up). Rebuild the surface BufferGeometry reactively on every equation parse; clamp/ignore NaN outside the plotted domain and keep the surface clipped to a sensible z-range. The column top must track f at the dragged (x*_k, y*_k); if the sample point is dragged outside the base region, clamp it to the region boundary. Reserve pointer-drag exclusively for the sample point (no orbit) to avoid gesture conflict; render the column with depthWrite off and transparent sorting so the dashed centerline and dots stay visible through it. Update the three numeric readouts (Height, Volume, Area) as HTML overlays or sprite labels each frame.

authoredContext:
The procedure for finding the volume V of the solid in Figure 14.1.1 will be similar to
the limiting process used for finding areas, except that now the approximating elements
will be rectangular parallelepipeds rather than rectangles. We proceed as follows: ..... Choose any arbitrary point in each subrectangle, and denote the point in the kth subrectangle by (x∗ k ,y∗ k ). As shown in Figure 14.1.3, the product f (x∗ k ,y∗ k )_x000b_Ak is the volume of a rectangular parallelepiped with base area _x000b_Ak and height f (x∗ k ,y∗ k ), so the sum #n k=1 f (x∗ k ,y∗ k )_x000b_Ak can be viewed as an approximation to the volume V of the entire solid.

Dragging the sample point (x*_k, y*_k) across the gridded base relocates the orange column and updates its height to f at that location, showing that each subrectangle contributes its own sampled height f(x*_k, y*_k)·ΔA_k to the total volume

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale 1 unit = 1. Base region is a peanut/kidney shape roughly spanning x ∈ [-1.4, 1.4], y ∈ [-1.2, 1.2] in the xy-plane (z=0), drawn as a closed teal-green outline #1aa88a with an interior grid of grey partition lines (Δx = Δy ≈ 0.4). The highlighted subrectangle sits near front-center at about (x*_k, y*_k) = (0.3, 0.2) with ΔA_k = 0.16. Default surface f(x,y) = 2 - x^2 - y^2 (peak 2 at origin, zero at radius √2 ≈ 1.41); render as a translucent teal mesh #7fd4d4 at ~0.45 opacity over x,y ∈ [-1.5,1.5]. The orange column #f0a840 (~0.45 opacity) rises from the subrectangle (footprint 0.4 × 0.4) up to z = f(x*_k, y*_k) ≈ 1.87 by default. Red dashed centerline #e03020 with red sphere dots (radius ~0.05) at top (on surface) and base. Axes black with arrowheads; z up to ~2.5, x and y to ~±2. Displayed readouts: Height = f(x*_k,y*_k), Volume = f(x*_k,y*_k)·ΔA_k, Area = ΔA_k, updated live. Annotation arrows are thin black curved lines from each text label to its target.
interactionPlan.notes: Use a standard isometric/axonometric pose matching the source (x toward lower-left, y right, z up). Rebuild the surface BufferGeometry reactively on every equation parse; clamp/ignore NaN outside the plotted domain and keep the surface clipped to a sensible z-range. The column top must track f at the dragged (x*_k, y*_k); if the sample point is dragged outside the base region, clamp it to the region boundary. Reserve pointer-drag exclusively for the sample point (no orbit) to avoid gesture conflict; render the column with depthWrite off and transparent sorting so the dashed centerline and dots stay visible through it. Update the three numeric readouts (Height, Volume, Area) as HTML overlays or sprite labels each frame.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure shows a 3D diagram illustrating the Riemann sum approximation used to define the double integral as a volume. A curved surface z = f(x, y) is shown in xyz-space above a region in the xy-plane; the base is gridded to represent a partition into subrectangles. A single representative rectangular parallelepiped is highlighted in orange: its base is a subrectangle with area Delta_Ak and sampling point (x*_k, y*_k) labeled, and its height is f(x*_k, y*_k), giving volume f(x*_k, y*_k) Delta_Ak. Annotations label Height f(x*_k, y*_k), Volume f(x*_k, y*_k) Delta_Ak, and Area Delta_Ak. The figure introduces the double integral as the limit of a Riemann sum of such parallelepiped volumes over all subrectangles as the partition is refined.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- equation input for f(x, y): one field pre-filled with a simple function (e.g. "2 - x*x - y*y"); learner edits it and the 3D surface z=f(x,y) redraws, the column height f(xk*,yk*) updates, and the displayed volume estimate f(xk*,yk*)·ΔAk refreshes — shows directly how the integrand determines the height of every approximating column
- drag the sample point (xk*, yk*) across the base region to move the column and read off f(xk*, yk*) at that location
plan.sourcePath: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.1.3
